new_statements.quote: Most of the word stress in the Embaloh language is located on the right (right edge). However, the stress is not distinctive or distinguishes the lexical meaning. The location of the lexical stress in the Embaloh language is generally in the final syllable. [...] In the Embaloh language, stress is generally consistent at the final syllable. The stress does not shift when the target word is affixed. [...] (1) a. [bu'kut] 'punch' [mamu'kut] 'to punch' b. [ju'lu] 'push' [julu'ang] 'to push' [taju'lu] 'pushed' [...] This finding also differs from Adelaar (1995), which stated that word stress location in the Embaloh language was at the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (non-contrastive) falls on the final syllable of the word, including affixed/suffixed forms (stress stays word-final, i.e. moves onto a suffix); realised as an L-to-H rise of c. 3-4 semitones plus greater duration/intensity; the language is not tonal. NOTE: the older primary description (Adelaar 1995, as reported by these authors and by Buu 2009) says penultimate; the 2024 instrumental study explicitly contradicts it.
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level (stress 'generally'/'tends to be' final; number of syllables and affixation do not affect it). At phrase level: in yes/no questions with the obligatory final particle ka and in statements with the enclitic -lah, the nuclear pitch accent sits on the last syllable of the pre-final word rather than utterance-finally.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical level analysed from elicited words (Swadesh-based list, 449 items) and words in carrier/spontaneous utterances from 12 speakers of Banua Ujung (Embaloh Hulu); authors separate word stress from post-lexical pitch accent, but word-level evidence is F0/duration on words that may be utterance-final, so a boundary-tone confound is possible. Contradiction with Adelaar 1995 (penultimate) is acknowledged by the authors; Adelaar's own wording not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Irawan et al. 2024 recorded speakers in Banua Ujung village, Embaloh Hulu subdistrict, Kapuas Hulu (the Embaloh-river variety = Tamambaloh); same language as Glottolog emba1238 / ISO emb (also called Maloh). Adelaar's 1995 data are also Embaloh proper. No dialect split is coded in Glottolog.

sources.note: Instrumental (Praat, AM framework, 12 speakers, Banua Ujung / Embaloh Hulu): word stress is non-distinctive and falls on the FINAL syllable, does not shift under affixation ([bu'kut] ~ [mamu'kut], [ju'lu] ~ [julu'ang] ~ [taju'lu]); language classed as fixed-stress, right-edge, not tonal (pp. 29-30, 35, 37). Also reports (p. 25) that Adelaar 1995 and Buu 2009 give penultimate non-distinctive stress, and explicitly says its finding differs from Adelaar 1995 (p. 35).
